analogy.p: Imagine a hall in which a known number of dancers (the alkali in the flask) each need exactly one partner. A volunteer (the burette) lets partners in one at a time, and the dance teacher blows a whistle (the indicator changing colour) the instant the last dancer has a partner. The number of partners let in tells you how many dancers there were. For H₂SO₄ and NaOH each acid 'dancer' needs two alkali partners, which is why the 1 : 2 ratio matters. The analogy breaks down because ions are not counted individually: you measure a volume of solution and calculate the number of particles from its concentration.

bullets: The reaction is a **neutralisation**: acid + alkali → salt + water, e.g. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.
An **indicator** shows the **end point**, the moment the acid and alkali have reacted exactly in the ratio shown by the equation.
The result of the practical is the **titre**, the volume (in cm³) of solution run from the burette.
Titration calculations belong to **separate chemistry (triple) only**, and the calculations are **Higher tier** content.
Industry uses titrations for quality control, e.g. checking acid levels in food, water and medicines.
The practical is a **required practical**, so you may be asked about the method, the apparatus or the results.
core.h: What a titration is and why it is used
core.p: A **titration** is a method that finds the **exact volume** of one solution needed to react completely with a known volume of another solution. In the GCSE version you use a **strong acid** and a **strong alkali** (for example hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide). If you know the concentration of one solution, the volumes and the **balanced equation** let you work out the unknown concentration. Titrations are used because they give very **precise** volume measurements, which cannot be done by simply mixing and testing with litmus paper.

bullets: **1 dm³ = 1000 cm³**, so volume in dm³ = volume in cm³ ÷ 1000.
Concentration is measured in **mol/dm³** (amount) or **g/dm³** (mass).
**Moles** (mol) measure amount of substance; **Mr** is the relative formula mass (no units).
Mass (g) = moles × Mr and moles = mass ÷ Mr.
Keep numbers in your calculator memory or to **at least 4 significant figures** until the final answer, then round.
core.h: Units and conversions you must be fluent in
core.p: Almost every mistake in titration calculations is a **units error**. Volumes in the lab are measured in **cm³** but concentrations in mol/dm³ need volumes in **dm³**. One **dm³ equals 1000 cm³**, so you divide a volume in cm³ by 1000 to get dm³. A dm³ is the same as a litre. Always convert the volume **first**, before you start the rest of the calculation, and write the converted value down so the examiner can see it.

bullets: **Concentration (g/dm³) = mass of solute (g) ÷ volume of solution (dm³)**.
**Concentration (mol/dm³) = moles of solute ÷ volume of solution (dm³)**.
Rearranged: **moles = concentration (mol/dm³) × volume (dm³)**.
**mol/dm³ → g/dm³: multiply by Mr**; **g/dm³ → mol/dm³: divide by Mr**.
Example: 4.00 g/dm³ of NaOH (Mr 40) = 4.00 ÷ 40 = 0.100 mol/dm³.
Doubling the concentration doubles the number of moles in a given volume; a more dilute solution therefore needs a larger titre to supply the same number of moles.
core.p: The **concentration** of a solution tells you how much solute is dissolved in a given volume of solution. It can be given as a **mass** per volume (g/dm³) or as an **amount in moles** per volume (mol/dm³). A concentrated solution has a lot of solute in a small volume; a dilute solution has little. Because chemical reactions depend on the **number of particles** (moles) rather than mass, titration calculations are done in mol/dm³, and then converted to g/dm³ if the question asks.

bullets: **Pipette** with a **pipette filler**: measures exactly 25.0 cm³ of the solution in the flask; never suck by mouth.
**Burette**: long graduated tube with a tap, used to add the other solution gradually and measure its volume.
**Conical flask**: its sloping sides let you **swirl** without spilling, and the narrow neck reduces splashing.
**White tile** under the flask makes the colour change at the end point easy to see.
**Funnel**: used only to fill the burette; it is **removed** afterwards so a stray drop does not fall in and change the reading.
**Indicator** (a few drops): too much indicator is itself a weak acid or alkali and can affect the result.
core.h: The apparatus and why each piece is chosen
core.p: Each piece of apparatus in a titration has a particular job, and examiners reward you for giving the **reason** for the choice. The **pipette** measures a **fixed volume** (usually 25.0 cm³) of one solution very accurately, because it has only one calibration mark. The **burette** delivers a **variable volume** that can be read to the nearest 0.05 cm³ and released one drop at a time. A measuring cylinder is much less accurate and is **not** used for the volumes that matter in a titration.

bullets: **Phenolphthalein**: **pink in alkali**, **colourless in acid**; the end point is when the pink just disappears (or just appears).
**Methyl orange**: **yellow in alkali**, **red in acid**; the end point is the first **orange** colour.
Indicators work because their molecules are **weak acids or bases** that change structure and colour when the pH changes.
A pH meter or probe could be used instead of an indicator; the data gives a **titration curve** (see below).
Record the colour in the flask **before** and **after** the end point in your results.
For a strong acid and strong alkali, the **neutral point (pH 7)** lies in the middle of the steep section of the curve.
core.p: An **indicator** is a substance that changes colour depending on the pH of the solution. For a titration you need an indicator with a **sharp, distinct colour change** exactly at the end point. **Phenolphthalein** and **methyl orange** are suitable for strong acid with strong alkali because the pH changes very rapidly from about 3 to 11 with a single drop. **Universal indicator** is **not suitable** because it changes through many colours gradually, so the exact end point is hard to judge.

bullets: 1. **Rinse** the pipette with the alkali and the burette with the acid (so the solutions are not diluted by leftover water).
2. Use the pipette and filler to transfer **25.0 cm³ of alkali** into a clean conical flask; add **2 to 3 drops of indicator**.
3. Fill the burette with acid using a funnel, **remove the funnel**, fill the tip below the tap, and record the **initial reading** at the **bottom of the meniscus at eye level**.
4. Stand the flask on a **white tile** under the burette; add acid **slowly**, **swirling** the flask continuously.
5. Do a **rough titration** first, then repeat adding the acid **dropwise** when close to the rough value.
6. Stop at the **end point** (a single drop causes a permanent colour change); record the **final reading**.
7. **Titre = final reading − initial reading**; repeat until you have **concordant results**.
core.h: Method: carrying out a titration (required practical)
core.p: The method must be learned in order, because 4 or 6 mark questions ask you to **describe it**. You first rinse the apparatus, then use the pipette to put a known volume of one solution in the flask, add indicator, and then add the other solution from the burette until the colour just changes. Doing a quick **rough titration** first saves time and reduces waste, because you then know approximately where the end point is.

bullets: The titre is **always** the **difference** between two burette readings, not the final reading alone.
Burette readings are recorded to **two decimal places**, ending in 0 or 5 (for example 22.45 cm³), because the scale is read to the nearest half division, 0.05 cm³.
If the results are not concordant, **repeat** the titration until at least two or three agree.
An **anomalous** result is one that does not fit the pattern; it is **identified and ignored** in the mean.
Adding the last bit of acid **dropwise** (even half a drop, washed down with distilled water) avoids overshooting the end point.
**Overshooting** the end point gives a titre that is too large, so the calculated concentration of the unknown is wrong.
core.h: End point, titre, rough titre and concordant results
core.p: The **end point** is the point when the indicator permanently changes colour, showing that the acid and alkali have reacted completely in the exact ratio from the equation. The **titre** is the volume of solution added from the burette to reach it. The **rough** titre is only used as a guide and is **never** included in the mean. To have confidence in a result, you need **concordant results**, which are titres within **0.10 cm³** of each other, and you calculate the **mean of the concordant titres only**.

bullets: Use headings such as **Initial reading (cm³)**, **Final reading (cm³)** and **Titre (cm³)**.
Calculate **titre = final − initial** for each run before averaging.
Example: titres 22.55, 22.50, 22.45 cm³ are all within 0.10 of each other so mean = (22.55 + 22.50 + 22.45) ÷ 3 = **22.50 cm³**.
Do **not** include the rough titre (23.40 cm³ in the example) or any anomalous value.
State the mean to **the same number of decimal places as the readings** (two).
Using the mean reduces the effect of **random errors** and makes the result more **reliable**.
core.p: Titration results should be recorded in a **table** with headings that include **units** and with the readings written to **two decimal places**. The table normally has columns for rough, trial 1, trial 2, trial 3 and rows for the initial reading, final reading and titre. The **mean titre** is calculated from the concordant results. This mean is the value used in the calculation, and it is shown as the volume of solution from the burette.

bullets: Step 1: write the **balanced equation** and note the **mole ratio** (for HCl + NaOH it is 1 : 1).
Step 2: **moles of known = concentration (mol/dm³) × volume (dm³)** (convert cm³ to dm³ by ÷ 1000).
Step 3: use the **ratio** to find moles of the unknown substance.
Step 4: **concentration of unknown (mol/dm³) = moles ÷ volume of unknown (dm³)**.
Step 5 (if asked): **concentration in g/dm³ = mol/dm³ × Mr**.
Give the final answer to the **correct significant figures** (usually 3) with the **unit** (mol/dm³ or g/dm³).
Check: if the volumes are similar and the ratio is 1 : 1, the two concentrations should be **similar**.
core.p: Titration calculation questions normally earn 4 to 5 marks, one for each step shown. The method is always the same: calculate **moles of the solution whose concentration you know**, use the **balanced equation** to find moles of the other substance, then divide by its volume. Always write each step, with units, and state the equation ratio you used. If you make a slip, the examiner can still give **error carried forward** marks for correct later steps.

bullets: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O: **moles NaOH = 2 × moles H₂SO₄**.
2HCl + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O: moles HCl = 2 × moles Ca(OH)₂.
Write the ratio explicitly, for example **mole ratio H₂SO₄ : NaOH = 1 : 2**.
To go from the **alkali to the acid** in H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH, **divide** the moles by 2.
To go from the **acid to the alkali**, **multiply** the moles by 2.
A balanced equation is therefore essential; if the question does not give it, you may need to write it.
core.p: Many questions use an equation where the substances do not react in a 1 : 1 ratio, and this is where candidates lose marks. The **big numbers** in the balanced equation give the ratio in which **moles** react. For sulfuric acid and sodium hydroxide, 1 mole of H₂SO₄ reacts with 2 moles of NaOH. If you forget this, your answer will be wrong by a factor of 2. Always compare the **moles**, never the concentrations or volumes directly.

bullets: **g/dm³ = mol/dm³ × Mr**; for 0.0900 mol/dm³ NaOH (Mr 40) this is **3.60 g/dm³**.
**Mass of solute = concentration (g/dm³) × volume (dm³)**, or moles × Mr.
A **dilution** keeps moles constant: c₁V₁ = c₂V₂ is a useful check, but derive it from moles = c × V.
To find an unknown acid concentration, swap the roles of the acid and alkali in the same method.
Use relative atomic masses from the Periodic Table: H = 1, O = 16, Na = 23, S = 32, Cl = 35.5.
core.h: Finding mass, g/dm³ and amounts in a sample
core.p: Questions often continue after finding the concentration in mol/dm³ and ask for the concentration in g/dm³ or the **mass of solute** in a stated volume. The route is simple if you remember the three links: moles ↔ mass using Mr, moles ↔ concentration using volume, and cm³ ↔ dm³ with ÷ 1000. You may also be asked to compare two titration results or to give the **purity** of a substance, which uses mass found ÷ mass of sample × 100.

bullets: The **resolution** of a burette is 0.1 cm³ (scale), read to ±0.05 cm³.
**Random errors** (e.g. judging the colour change) are reduced by **repeating** and calculating a mean.
**Systematic errors** (e.g. burette not rinsed with the acid so it is diluted, or the burette tip not filled) shift all results the same way.
An **air bubble** in the burette tip gives a titre that seems too big, as the bubble is later expelled.
Reading the **top** of the meniscus or reading from above/below eye level (**parallax error**) gives wrong readings.
Adding **too much indicator** or overshooting the end point makes the titre too large.
Rinsing the conical flask with **distilled water** does **not** matter because it does not change the moles of alkali in it.
core.p: Evaluating a titration involves understanding why some results are better than others. A result is **accurate** if close to the true value, **precise** if repeated readings are close together, **repeatable** if the same person gets the same results with the same method and equipment, and **reproducible** if different people or equipment give the same results. Using a pipette and burette rather than measuring cylinders gives **better resolution** and therefore a more accurate and precise result.

bullets: Wear **eye protection** (goggles) because acids and alkalis can damage eyes.
If you spill acid or alkali on skin, **wash with plenty of cold water**.
Use a **pipette filler**, never mouth pipetting, because the solutions are harmful if swallowed.
Clamp the burette securely to prevent it tipping, and **mop up spills** to avoid slipping.
**Control variables**: the same volume (25.0 cm³) of solution in the flask, the same indicator and number of drops, and the same solutions.
Repeat runs use identical conditions, so the aim is **repeatability**: the titres should agree within 0.10 cm³.
core.p: Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide at the concentrations used in school are **irritants**, and stronger solutions are **corrosive**. Appropriate precautions reduce the risk of harm, and examiners expect a precaution that is **linked to the hazard**. The glassware is fragile, and spillages must be wiped up. Controlling variables ensures that a change in titre is caused only by a change in concentration.

bullets: The **end point** is at the **middle of the steep section**, pH 7 for strong acid and strong alkali.
Before the end point the flask contains **excess acid** (pH below 7); after it, **excess alkali** (pH above 7).
The steep section is why both **phenolphthalein** and **methyl orange** are suitable.
Reading the volume off at **pH 7** gives the titre; draw construction lines on the graph.
The shape reflects the **logarithmic** nature of the pH scale: each pH unit is a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration.
Link: acids produce **H⁺ ions** and alkalis produce **OH⁻ ions**; neutralisation is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.
core.h: pH curves and the link to titration
core.p: If a pH meter is used, a graph of **pH against volume of alkali added** gives the **titration curve**. For a strong acid with a strong alkali, the pH starts low (about 1), rises slowly, then increases **very sharply** over a tiny volume at the end point, ending at a high pH (about 13). The **vertical section** is why a single drop of alkali causes a big colour change in the indicator. The curve tells you the volume needed to neutralise, which is the titre.

bullets: Link to **moles**: the calculation is based on the idea that substances react in the ratios of their moles.
Link to **salts**: the solution at the end point contains only the salt (e.g. sodium chloride) and water.
Link to **limiting reactants**: at the end point there is no excess of either reactant.
Link to **gas volumes**: the same moles ↔ quantity route is used (moles × 24 dm³ for gases).
Link to **required practical skills**: reading scales, recording, mean, uncertainty, safety.
Link to **atom economy and yield**: they all use the balanced equation to compare quantities.
core.p: Titration brings together many ideas from the specification, which is why it is such a common source of long questions. It uses **moles and balanced equations** from quantitative chemistry, **neutralisation and salts** from chemical changes, **indicators and the pH scale**, **concentration** and **practical skills** such as accuracy and uncertainty. In **analysis and rates** topics, similar ideas appear when interpreting concordant data and evaluating methods. In unfamiliar contexts (e.g. vinegar, bleach, antacid tablets) the **same five steps** apply.

exam: **Calculate** questions: show every step; marks are for moles of known, ratio, moles of unknown, concentration, and correct unit; **error carried forward** is allowed.
Titration calculation is usually **4 or 5 marks**; the answer alone with no working may score only 1 or 2 marks.
**Describe how to carry out a titration** (6 marks): rinse, pipette 25.0 cm³ with filler, indicator, burette filled, tile, swirl, add dropwise at end, record, repeat to concordant, mean.
**Why use a pipette rather than a measuring cylinder?** It measures a fixed volume more accurately (smaller uncertainty).
**Why do a rough titration first?** To find the approximate end point so that later titrations can add acid dropwise near it.
**Why repeat?** To check results are concordant and to reduce the effect of random errors (more reliable mean).
**State the colour change**: phenolphthalein pink to colourless (acid in burette), methyl orange yellow to orange/red; name the colours before and after.
**Explain why the mean omits anomalous results**: they are not representative and would reduce accuracy.
**Evaluate** questions: name an error (overshoot, air bubble, parallax) and say how it affects the titre and the calculated concentration.
For **graph** questions, draw construction lines at the steep section to find the volume at pH 7.
Give answers to the **same number of significant figures** as the data (usually 3 s.f.).
Command words: **calculate** (numerical working), **describe** (what you do), **explain** (give a reason using 'because'), **evaluate** (strengths and weaknesses then a judgement).

mistakes.r: Convert cm³ to dm³ first by dividing by 1000, then calculate moles.
mistakes.w: Using volumes in cm³ directly in moles = concentration × volume.

mistakes.r: Use the big numbers in the balanced equation to convert moles of one substance to moles of the other.
mistakes.w: Ignoring the ratio in the equation (e.g. H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH) and assuming 1 : 1.

mistakes.r: Use only concordant results (within 0.10 cm³) and ignore the rough titre and any anomalies.
mistakes.w: Including the rough titre in the mean.

mistakes.r: Read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level.
mistakes.w: Reading the top of the meniscus, or reading from above or below.

mistakes.r: Use phenolphthalein or methyl orange for a sharp colour change; universal indicator changes gradually.
mistakes.w: Using universal indicator because it shows all colours.

mistakes.r: A pipette measures a fixed volume with much greater accuracy and precision.
mistakes.w: Saying a measuring cylinder is as good as a pipette.
Giving the final reading as the titre.

mistakes.r: Multiply by Mr for g/dm³ and always include the unit.
mistakes.w: Giving the answer in mol/dm³ when g/dm³ was asked, or without units.

mistakes.r: State that at the end point the acid and alkali have reacted exactly in the ratio shown by the equation.
mistakes.w: Saying the colour change shows the solution is 'neutral' without saying the end point is when reaction is complete.

summary: You must be able to describe the titration practical (strong acid with strong alkali), record and process results, and (Higher tier, triple) calculate unknown concentrations in mol/dm³ and g/dm³ from titre volumes using balanced equations. It matters because it is a required practical and gives long, multi-mark calculation questions.

terms.d: A method to find the volume of one solution that reacts exactly with a known volume of another solution, used to find an unknown concentration.
The reaction of an acid with an alkali (or base) to form a salt and water; H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.
Graduated glass tube with a tap, used to add a variable volume of solution accurately, drop by drop.
Apparatus used to measure and transfer a fixed volume of solution (e.g. 25.0 cm³) very accurately, used with a pipette filler.
A substance that changes colour depending on the pH of the solution, used to show the end point.
The point at which the indicator permanently changes colour, showing the reaction is exactly complete.
The volume of solution added from the burette to reach the end point (final reading minus initial reading).
A first quick titration used only as a guide to where the end point is; it is not used in the mean.
Results that are close together, within 0.10 cm³ of each other.
The amount of solute dissolved in a given volume of solution, in g/dm³ or mol/dm³.
The unit for the amount of a substance; one mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles and has a mass equal to its Mr in grams.
The curved upper surface of a liquid in a narrow tube; burette readings are taken at the bottom of it at eye level.
A measurement that is close to the true value.
Repeated measurements that are close together (small spread).
The same person gets the same results using the same method and equipment.
Different people or different equipment or methods give the same results.

worked.q: 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution is neutralised by 22.50 cm³ of hydrochloric acid of concentration 0.100 mol/dm³. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide in mol/dm³ and in g/dm³. Ar: Na 23, O 16, H 1. (5 marks)
steps: Mole ratio HCl : NaOH = 1 : 1, so moles NaOH = 0.002250 mol.

worked.q: 20.0 cm³ of sulfuric acid is neutralised by 24.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide of concentration 0.150 mol/dm³. H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the sulfuric acid in mol/dm³ and g/dm³. Mr H₂SO₄ = 98. (5 marks)
steps: Ratio H₂SO₄ : NaOH = 1 : 2, so moles H₂SO₄ = 0.00360 ÷ 2 = 0.00180 mol.

worked.ans: Model answer: pipette 25.0 cm³ alkali + indicator in flask on white tile; add acid from burette swirling; rough then dropwise near the end point; record titre; repeat until concordant; mean of concordant results.
worked.q: Describe how you would carry out a titration to find the volume of hydrochloric acid needed to neutralise 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution. (6 marks)
steps: Rinse the pipette with sodium hydroxide and the burette with acid.
Use a pipette and pipette filler to add 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide to a conical flask, then add a few drops of indicator (e.g. phenolphthalein, pink in alkali).
Fill the burette with acid, remove the funnel and record the initial reading at the bottom of the meniscus.
Place the flask on a white tile; add acid slowly while swirling, doing a rough titration first.
Repeat, adding acid dropwise near the end point until the indicator just changes permanently (pink to colourless); record the final reading.
Titre = final − initial; repeat until results are concordant (within 0.10 cm³) and calculate the mean of concordant titres.
